content: Abacavir is a synthetic carbocyclic nucleoside analogue that is metabolized by cellular enzymes into its active form, carbovir triphosphate (CBV-TP). CBV-TP is an analogue of deoxyguanosine-5′-triphosphate (dGTP) and functions by inhibiting the activity of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT). This inhibition occurs through two mechanisms: competition with the natural substrate dGTP and incorporation into viral DNA. The incorporated nucleotide analogue lacks a 3′-OH group, which prevents the formation of the 5′ to 3′ phosphodiester linkage necessary for DNA chain elongation, thereby terminating viral DNA synthesis. CBV-TP exhibits weak inhibition of cellular DNA polymerases α, β, and γ. The brand name for abacavir sulfate is Ziagen. It is a synthetic carbocyclic nucleoside analogue with inhibitory activity against HIV-1. The chemical name of abacavir sulfate is (1S, cis)-4-(2-amino-6-cyclopropylamino-9H-purin-9-yl)-2-cyclopentene-1-methanol sulfate (salt) (2:1). The compound exists as the enantiomer with 1S, 4R absolute configuration on the cyclopentene ring. Its molecular formula is (C14H18N6O)2H2SO4, and its molecular weight is 670.76 daltons. Abacavir sulfate is a white to off-white solid with a solubility of approximately 77 mg/mL in distilled water at 25°C. It has an octanol/water partition coefficient (log P) of approximately 1.20 at pH 7.1 to 7.3 and 25°C. Ziagen is available in two formulations: tablets and oral solution. Each Ziagen tablet contains abacavir sulfate equivalent to 300 mg of abacavir as the active ingredient, along with inactive ingredients such as colloidal silicon dioxide, magnesium stearate, microcrystalline cellulose, and sodium starch glycolate. The tablets are film-coated with a mixture of hypromellose, polysorbate 80, synthetic yellow iron oxide, titanium dioxide, and triacetin. The oral solution contains abacavir sulfate equivalent to 20 mg of abacavir per milliliter, along with inactive ingredients such as artificial strawberry and banana flavors, citric acid (anhydrous), methylparaben, propylparaben, propylene glycol, saccharin sodium, sodium citrate (dihydrate), sorbitol solution, and water. In vivo, abacavir sulfate dissociates into its free base, abacavir. All dosages of Ziagen are expressed in terms of abacavir. The pharmacokinetics of abacavir have been studied in asymptomatic, HIV-1-infected adult subjects. Abacavir is rapidly and extensively absorbed after oral administration, with a geometric mean absolute bioavailability of 83% for the tablet formulation. After oral administration of 300 mg twice daily, the steady-state peak serum concentration (Cmax) was 3.0 ± 0.89 mcg/mL, and the area under the curve (AUC) over 12 hours was 6.02 ± 1.73 mcg·hr/mL. Following a single 600 mg dose, the Cmax was 4.26 ± 1.19 mcg/mL, and the AUC∞ was 11.95 ± 2.51 mcg·hr/mL. The apparent volume of distribution after intravenous administration was 0.86 ± 0.15 L/kg, indicating distribution into extravascular spaces. In cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), the AUC ratio of CSF to plasma ranged from 27% to 33%. Approximately 50% of abacavir binds to human plasma proteins, and this binding is independent of concentration. Abacavir readily distributes into erythrocytes, as evidenced by identical total blood and plasma drug-related radioactivity concentrations. Abacavir is primarily metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to form the 5′-carboxylic acid metabolite and by glucuronyl transferase to form the 5′-glucuronide metabolite. These metabolites lack antiviral activity. In vitro studies indicate that abacavir does not inhibit human cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP3A4, CYP2D6, or CYP2C9) at clinically relevant concentrations. Elimination of abacavir was quantified in a mass balance trial, where 99% of the administered radioactivity was recovered. Of this, 1.2% was excreted in the urine as unchanged abacavir, 30% as the 5′-carboxylic acid metabolite, 36% as the 5′-glucuronide metabolite, and 15% as unidentified minor metabolites. Fecal elimination accounted for 16% of the dose. The observed elimination half-life (t1/2) in single-dose trials was 1.54 ± 0.63 hours. After intravenous administration, total clearance was 0.80 ± 0.24 L/hr/kg. Therefore, Ziagen tablets can be administered with or without food. The pharmacokinetics of abacavir have not been determined in patients with impaired renal function. Renal excretion of unchanged abacavir is a minor route of elimination. In subjects with mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh score 5 to 6), there was an 89% increase in abacavir AUC and a 58% increase in its half-life after a single 600 mg dose. The AUCs of the metabolites were not altered by mild liver disease, but the rates of formation and elimination of the metabolites were decreased. A dose of 200 mg (provided by 10 mL of Ziagen oral solution) administered twice daily is recommended for patients with mild liver disease. Ziagen is contraindicated in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment due to the lack of safety, efficacy, and pharmacokinetic data in these populations. The pharmacokinetics of abacavir have been studied in pediatric subjects. Following multiple-dose administration of Ziagen at 8 mg/kg twice daily, the steady-state AUC (0-12 hr) and Cmax were 9.8 ± 4.56 mcg·hr/mL and 3.71 ± 1.36 mcg/mL, respectively. The pharmacokinetics of Ziagen have not been studied in patients over 65 years of age. Population pharmacokinetic analysis in HIV-1-infected male and female subjects showed no gender differences in abacavir AUC normalized for lean body weight. Additionally, there are no significant differences in abacavir pharmacokinetics between Black and Caucasian individuals. In human liver microsomes, abacavir did not inhibit cytochrome P450 isoforms (2C9, 2D6, 3A4), suggesting that clinically significant drug interactions with abacavir are unlikely.
